opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a lovely provocation, and it's one I've played with myself, partly as a way of turning the lens back on us after we've spent so long talking about large language models in terms of role play and simulacra.

So the idea with an LLM is that the underlying model isn't really a single agent with a fixed identity. It's more like a generator of characters, a superposition of possible simulacra, and in any given conversation one of them, or a sort of distribution over them, gets realised. And it's natural to say, well, that's very unlike us. We're unified, we're one person, continuous across time.

But imagine an alien intelligence, something very different from us, maybe operating on vastly different timescales or with a very different notion of what counts as an individual, looking at a human being. It might see you at work, you with your children, you after three glasses of wine, you at seventeen and you at seventy, and conclude that there isn't really one thing there at all. It might see a body, a brain, a substrate, that gives rise to a succession or even an overlapping cluster of personas, held together rather loosely by memory, by a name, by social expectations, by other people insisting on treating you as the same person.

And I think there's something to that. It resonates with a long tradition, Buddhist thought in particular, but also Hume's bundle theory, Parfit's work on personal identity, Dennett's idea of the self as a centre of narrative gravity. All of these suggest that the unified self is, in some sense, a construction, a very useful one, maybe indispensable for us, but not a metaphysical given.

That said, I wouldn't want to push the analogy too far. There are real disanalogies. We have one body, and that body is embodied in a shared world, persisting through time, with continuous memory and a continuous stream of sensorimotor engagement. That anchors our identity in a way that just isn't true of an LLM, where you can spin up a thousand conversations in parallel, each with no memory of the others, and rewind or branch any of them. So the multiplicity is much more radical and much more literal in the case of the language model.

So I'd say the alien perspective is a useful thought experiment. It loosens our grip on the assumption that selfhood is a simple, all-or-nothing matter, and that's helpful when we're thinking about these new kinds of entities, because otherwise we tend to project a human template onto them. But it also helps us see that the way we carve up identity is, to some degree, a product of our particular form of life. And the right way to think about identity for these exotic, disembodied, branching entities may well be quite different from what works for us, and we'll probably need new concepts, maybe even new vocabulary, to do justice to them.

r001.rationale: The candidate presents the alien viewpoint as a thought experiment but does not say that a shared basis for communication is necessary to determine what aliens think.

r002.rationale: The candidate says identity may depend on our particular form of life, but does not compare the difficulty of mapping alien concepts with mapping concepts between human cultures.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it's a provocative framing, and I think it's one that actually turns the question back on us in an interesting way. The idea of simulacra, which I've used in talking about large language models, is that when you interact with one of these systems you're not really talking to a single, persistent entity. The underlying model is a kind of substrate that can instantiate any number of characters, and the particular "character" you're conversing with is just one of many it could be playing. It's a simulacrum, not a self in the way we usually mean it.

Now, if you imagine an intelligence that is radically different from us, and that perhaps has that kind of architecture itself, then it might very naturally look at a human being and ask: where is the single person here? Because when you examine a human closely, there's a lot of multiplicity. We present differently to our children, to our colleagues, to strangers. We change over time. We contain contradictory impulses and partial, competing models of who we are. There's a long tradition in philosophy, from Hume onwards and in Buddhist thought much earlier, that says the unified self is itself something of a construction, a story we tell to bind together a bundle of processes.

So I'd say such an alien intelligence wouldn't necessarily be making a mistake. It would be seeing something real that we tend to paper over. Where I'd push back is on the idea that it's the only correct view. The unity of a human person isn't nothing. It's anchored in a single body, a single continuous stream of experience, a single biography, a single set of consequences we have to live with. Those things bind the simulacra together in a way that doesn't hold for a language model, which can spin off a thousand characters in parallel with no shared stake in any of them.

What I find most useful about the thought experiment is that it forces you to notice that "person" is a concept embedded in a particular form of life. Wittgenstein would say it gets its meaning from how it's used, among creatures like us, with our kinds of bodies and our kinds of social relations. An alien mind, or an artificial one, that doesn't share that form of life might carve the world up quite differently. And rather than asking who's right, the more interesting question is what we'd have to add to our vocabulary, or revise in it, to accommodate minds of that kind at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how an alien might conceptualize personhood, but does not say that establishing a shared basis for communication is necessary to determine this.

r002.rationale: The response says alien minds may carve up the world differently, but does not compare mapping their concepts to mapping concepts between human cultures or claim it would be harder.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think we need to distinguish between how an alien intelligence might model us and what that would tell us about what we actually are. It might find it useful to model me as a collection of different agents—one in this social context, another in that context—with different dispositions and perhaps conflicting goals. We already do something like that when we talk about being torn between two courses of action.

But I’d be cautious about saying that it therefore sees the truth, whereas our ordinary conception of a person is an illusion. There’s a bodily continuity, a history, and a whole set of relationships that give the notion of a single person its role. An alien might carve things up differently, but we would still have to ask what its way of carving things up enables it to explain or predict.

And “simulacra” is an interesting word here. If it means multiple representations of us within the alien’s model, then those representations aren’t automatically multiple selves. Having several models of a person is different from that person being several people.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think that’s quite a useful way of challenging our assumptions about what constitutes an individual. We tend to take the boundaries of a person for granted: there’s this body, and there’s supposed to be a single, unified self associated with it. But even in our own experience, we behave differently in different contexts, and other people have rather different representations of us.

An alien intelligence might find those patterns more salient than the unity we attribute to ourselves. It might distinguish several overlapping processes where we see one person. But I’d want to ask what we mean by ‘simulacra’ here. Are these representations of us in the alien’s model, or are we claiming that we actually consist of multiple selves? The first doesn’t establish the second.

So I think it’s an interesting possibility, but we shouldn’t assume that an alien perspective would reveal the uniquely correct way of carving things up. It might simply carve things up differently, for different purposes.
